hints: Focus on the size of the melting point drop, from 1883 K to 297 K, and ask what kind of structural change causes such a huge fall.
Remember that $\text{SiO}_2$ forms a giant covalent lattice with strong bonds in all directions, while $\text{P}_4\text{O}_6$ exists as separate small molecules.
Think about what must be broken to melt each one, strong covalent bonds throughout a lattice versus only weak intermolecular forces between molecules.
walkthrough:
**Look at the data**

The melting point falls dramatically from 1883 K for $\text{SiO}_2$ to only 297 K for $\text{P}_4\text{O}_6$. Such a large difference tells us the bonding or structure must be very different.

**Recall the structures of the two oxides**

$\text{SiO}_2$ has a giant molecular (giant covalent) structure. Every Si atom is covalently bonded to O atoms in a continuous 3D network.

$\text{P}_4\text{O}_6$ has a simple molecular structure. It exists as discrete $\text{P}_4\text{O}_6$ molecules held together only by weak van der Waals forces.

**Link structure to melting point**

To melt $\text{SiO}_2$, many strong Si-O covalent bonds must be broken. This needs a lot of energy, so the melting point is very high.

To melt $\text{P}_4\text{O}_6$, only weak intermolecular forces between molecules are broken. Covalent bonds inside the molecule stay intact. This needs little energy, so the melting point is low.

Therefore the change from giant molecular to simple molecular explains the difference.

options.A: Incorrect. Both $\text{SiO}_2$ and $\text{P}_4\text{O}_6$ are covalent oxides, not ionic. There is no change from ionic to covalent here, so this cannot explain the melting point drop.
options.B: Incorrect. It is true that metallic character decreases across Period 3, but this is a general periodic trend. It does not directly explain why so much less energy is needed to melt $\text{P}_4\text{O}_6$ than $\text{SiO}_2$.
options.C: Incorrect. The oxidation number does not increase. Si in $\text{SiO}_2$ is +4, while P in $\text{P}_4\text{O}_6$ is +3. More importantly, oxidation number does not control the strength of forces that must be broken on melting.
options.D: Correct. $\text{SiO}_2$ is giant molecular with a network of strong covalent bonds, requiring huge energy to break. $\text{P}_4\text{O}_6$ is simple molecular with only weak van der Waals forces between molecules, requiring little energy to overcome. This structural change perfectly explains the fall from 1883 K to 297 K.
